Giving fund units to charity instead of cash: how a gift in kind removes the tax on the gain

Compare donating mutual fund units directly with selling them and donating the cash, see what the donation credit is worth in each province, and test the step that resets your cost base if you want to keep holding the fund.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare giving fund units directly to a charity with selling them first and giving the cash

Units worth $20,000 with a $12,000 cost base are given to a registered charity. Either route earns the same official receipt for $20,000 and a 45.8% credit, $9,160. Selling first makes half of the $8,000 gain taxable at 40%; giving the units directly can qualify for a zero inclusion rate. The credit rate assumes your first CAD 200 of gifts this year is already claimed and that total gifts stay within 75% of net income. The fund return of 6% is a hypothetical input, not a forecast; this is not a personal tax calculation.

The central idea

When fund units in a non-registered account have risen above their cost, giving the units themselves to a registered charity can qualify for a zero capital-gains inclusion rate, while selling first makes half the gain taxable. The receipt and the donation credit are the same either way. The edge depends on the size of the gain, not on the fund, and disappears for units held in a TFSA or RRSP or bought near today’s price.

01

Two ways to give the same amount

Many people who give to charity each year also hold a balanced fund or an equity fund in a non-registered account. If that fund has grown, there are two ways to turn part of it into a gift. One is to sell units, pay any tax on the gain, and give the cash. The other is to ask the fund company or dealer to transfer the units themselves to the charity, which then sells them.

The charity ends up with the same money. The difference is on your tax return. CRA’s guide Gifts and Income Tax lists units of a mutual fund trust and shares of a mutual fund corporation among the properties for which a donor may be entitled to an inclusion rate of zero on the capital gain, reported on Form T1170. When the same units are sold first, the gain is an ordinary capital gain, and CRA’s capital gains guide shows half of it being taxable.

This guide prices that difference, shows where the credit rate comes from, and covers the related case where you want to give and still keep the fund.

02

The credit is the same either way, and it is large

The first chart shows the combined credit rate CRA lists for gifts above the first CAD 200 in the 2025 tax year: a federal rate of 29% plus each province’s rate. The combined rate runs from about 40% in Ontario to about 51% in Newfoundland and Labrador; British Columbia’s is 45.8%. Donors with income in the top federal bracket can claim 33% federally on the part of the gift covered by that income, and some provinces list a higher top rate too. Quebec’s credit is administered by Revenu Québec.

The credit is non-refundable: it reduces tax you would otherwise pay. CRA limits the gifts you can claim in a year to 75% of net income, and unused gifts can be carried forward up to five years. The model assumes the gift fits within that limit and that your first CAD 200 of gifts this year has already been claimed at the lower first-tier rate, so the whole gift earns the entered rate. Rates for 2026 returns may differ slightly, so check the current table before you file.

Because the receipt is for the fair market value of what the charity receives, the credit does not depend on whether you give units or cash. What changes is the tax on the gain.

03

Pricing the default case

The default gift is fund units worth CAD 20,000 with an adjusted cost base of CAD 12,000, so the units carry an unrealized gain of CAD 8,000. The combined credit rate is 45.8% and the marginal tax rate on capital gains income is 40%.

  • Either route: a receipt for CAD 20,000 and a credit of CAD 9,160.
  • Giving the units: no tax on the gain if the zero inclusion rate applies. Your net cost for a CAD 20,000 gift is CAD 10,840.
  • Selling first: half of the CAD 8,000 gain, CAD 4,000, is added to income and taxed at 40%, which is CAD 1,600. Your net cost for the same gift rises to CAD 12,440.

The second chart stacks those amounts. The heatmap repeats the comparison for cost bases from 0% to 100% of market value and marginal rates from 20% to 50%. Units with a cost base of 20% of their value save CAD 3,200 at a 40% rate; units bought near today’s price save almost nothing. A balanced fund held for many years, with distributions reinvested, often has a mix: the oldest purchases carry the largest gains, and the fund cost-base guide shows how reinvested distributions raise the cost base. For tax purposes, identical units of the same fund share one average cost base, so you cannot choose to give only the oldest, lowest-cost units.

04

Giving the units and buying the fund back

A common situation is a donor who planned to give cash from savings but likes the fund and wants to keep it. The third chart compares three routes that all give CAD 20,000 and all leave you holding CAD 20,000 of the same fund:

  1. Give your cash and keep the old units. No tax now, but the units keep their CAD 12,000 cost base.
  2. Give the units and use your cash to buy the fund again. No tax now, and the new units have a CAD 20,000 cost base.
  3. Sell the units, give the proceeds and rebuy with your cash. CAD 1,600 of tax now, and the new units also have a CAD 20,000 cost base.

With a 6% fund return, the after-tax value if everything is sold after 10 years is about CAD 32,654 for route 2, CAD 31,054 for route 1 and CAD 29,788 for route 3. Route 2 beats route 1 by the CAD 1,600 of tax that would otherwise be paid on the old gain at some later sale; route 3 is behind by the CAD 1,600 paid now plus the growth it gave up. The edge of route 2 over route 1 is a postponed tax that is never paid, so it matters most when the eventual sale is likely to happen at a similar or higher marginal rate.

Buying back the same fund after giving units at a gain does not run into the superficial-loss rule, which denies losses when identical property is bought within 30 days. That rule is explained in the fund tax-loss selling guide.

05

Which account the units are in matters more than which fund

The saving comes from the account’s tax rules, not from the fund. The benefit exists only for units held in a non-registered account, where a sale creates a taxable capital gain.

  • TFSA: gains are not taxed, so there is no gain to exempt. Withdrawing cash and giving it produces the same credit with no tax cost, and the withdrawal is added back to your room on 1 January of the next year.
  • RRSP or RRIF: money leaves the plan as a withdrawal, which is taxable income and subject to withholding. The donation credit can offset that tax, but there is no capital gain to exempt, so the in-kind advantage does not apply.
  • Units at a loss: with the value below cost there is no gain to exempt, and the model shows no difference between the routes. A loss on units that are sold is a capital loss you can use against other gains, as covered in the capital-loss carryback guide.

This also links the gift to capital-gain timing: units you planned to sell anyway in a high-income year are good candidates to give instead.

06

Practical steps and cautions

  1. Ask the charity first. CRA advises checking that an organization is a registered charity or other qualified donee before you give. Not every charity can receive fund units; many use a brokerage account or a donation platform. Gifts to a donor-advised fund at a public foundation are another route, with their own fees and rules.
  2. Transfer the units, do not sell them. The zero inclusion rate is for a gift of the property itself. A sale in your account followed by a cash gift is a sale. Leave several weeks before 31 December, because transfers between institutions take time and the gift counts in the year the charity receives it.
  3. Check fees and sales charges. Units bought with a deferred sales charge may trigger a redemption fee when the charity sells; that reduces the gift but not your tax saving.
  4. Keep the records. You need the official receipt for the fair market value on the date received, Form T1170 with your return, and your cost-base record for the units given.
  5. Fit the gift to your budget first. A tax saving makes a planned gift cheaper; it does not make an unplanned gift free. The charitable giving budget guide covers the cash side.

Special rules apply to flow-through shares, gifts with an advantage back to the donor, employee stock options and gifts by will. Those are outside this model; confirm a specific case with a tax professional.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. The first chart shows CRA’s published donation credit rates for the 2025 tax year, reviewed 27 October 2026. The zero inclusion rate for gifts of mutual fund units and the one-half inclusion rate on other capital gains are from CRA pages reviewed the same day. Gift values, cost bases, tax rates and fund returns in the other charts are hypothetical editable inputs, not a personal tax calculation or a forecast. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Canada Revenue Agency · P113, Gifts and Income Tax 2025 ↗

    Page dated 20 January 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026. Lists units of a mutual fund trust and shares of a mutual fund corporation among the properties for which a donor may be entitled to an inclusion rate of zero on the capital gain, with Form T1170 required for these gifts; the 75% of net income limit; and the five-year carryforward of unused gifts.

  2. Canada Revenue Agency · Line 34900, Donations and gifts: how much you can claim ↗

    Page dated 6 July 2026, for the 2025 tax year; reviewed 27 October 2026. Federal rates of 14.5%, 29% and 33%; provincial rates including British Columbia 5.06%, 16.8% and 20.5%, Ontario 5.05% and 11.16%, and Alberta 60% on the first CAD 200 and 21% above it. Used for the first chart and the default credit rate.

  3. Canada Revenue Agency · Calculating and reporting your capital gains and losses ↗

    Page dated 5 February 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026 for the statement that 50% of a capital gain is taxable, used as the one-half inclusion rate when units are sold first.

  4. Canada Revenue Agency · Before you give ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026 for the advice to confirm that an organization is a registered charity or other qualified donee before giving.
